This book covers AS topic 1 (atomic structure), topic 3 (chemical bonding) and topic 4 (states of matter), examined in Papers 1 and 2 and assumed throughout Paper 4. We use the Data Booklet values (for example R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Every calculation here was checked by computer. Mark guides are our own, in the Cambridge style: M1 = method, A1 = answer, B1 = independent point. They are not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: Protons, Neutrons, Electrons and Isotopes

Key ideas

  • Relative masses and charges: proton 1, +1; neutron 1, 0; electron 1/1836, −1.
  • Proton number Z = the number of protons; nucleon number A = protons + neutrons.
  • Isotopes: atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons; they have the same chemical properties (same electron configuration) but different physical properties (for example, density).
  • Beams in an electric field: protons deflect towards the negative plate, electrons (much larger deflection) towards the positive plate, neutrons are undeflected.
  • Ions: cations have lost electrons; anions have gained electrons.

Worked examples

Example 1: ³⁷Cl⁻ has 17 protons, 20 neutrons and 18 electrons.

Example 2: ²⁴Mg²⁺ has 12 protons, 12 neutrons and 10 electrons.

Example 3: electrons are deflected more than protons because their mass is much smaller (about 1/1836).

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Complete the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons for: (i) ⁴⁰Ca²⁺; (ii) ³²S²⁻; (iii) ¹⁸O. [3]

(b) Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties. [2]

(c) A beam containing protons, neutrons and electrons passes between charged plates. Describe and explain the behaviour of each particle. [3]

(d) Define relative isotopic mass. [2]

Answers and mark guide:

  • (a) (i) 20, 20, 18; (ii) 16, 16, 18; (iii) 8, 10, 8 (B1 each).
  • (b) They have the same number of electrons (B1) arranged in the same way, so they react in the same way (B1).
  • (c) Protons deflected towards the negative plate (B1); electrons deflected more, towards the positive plate, because they are much lighter (B1); neutrons undeflected as they are uncharged (B1).
  • (d) The mass of an atom of an isotope (B1) relative to one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12 (B1).

Common mistakes

  1. Electron counts for ions with the charge sign reversed.
  2. Saying isotopes have different chemical properties.
  3. Forgetting the "one-twelfth of carbon-12" standard.
  4. Deflection angles in the wrong order of size.
  5. Confusing nucleon number with proton number.

Quick recall

  1. Relative charge of a neutron?
  2. Electrons in Na⁺?
  3. What differs between isotopes?
  4. Standard for relative masses?
  5. Which particle is deflected most?

Answers: 1) 0. 2) 10. 3) The number of neutrons. 4) One-twelfth of the mass of a ¹²C atom. 5) The electron.
